◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Complex numbers complete algebra (every polynomial has roots) and unify trigonometry, exponentials, and rotation. They're indispensable in engineering, physics, and signal processing.

Complex number
z = a + bi with i² = −1. Modulus |z| = √(a² + b²); conjugate z̄ = a − bi; and z·z̄ = |z|². The argument arg(z) is the angle from the positive real axis.
WORKED EXAMPLE — multiplication and modulus

(2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i.

|3 + 4i| = √(9 + 16) = 5.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

i² = −1, so watch the sign when multiplying: −3i² = +3, not −3. This sign flip is where most arithmetic errors happen.

📊 FIGURE — A complex number lives in the plane
z = 3 + 4i sits 3 across and 4 up; its modulus |z| = √(3² + 4²) = 5 is the arrow’s length. The conjugate z̄ = 3 − 4i is the mirror image across the real axis — and z·z̄ = |z|² = 25, always real.
"}, "COMPLEX/ch1/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Euler's formula e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ is one of the most beautiful equations in mathematics — it turns multiplication of complex numbers into ROTATION, and makes powers and roots effortless.

Polar / Euler
z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r·e^{iθ}, where r = |z| and θ = arg(z). De Moivre: (e^{iθ})ⁿ = e^{inθ}, so zⁿ = rⁿe^{inθ} — powers scale the modulus and multiply the angle.
WORKED EXAMPLE — Euler's identity

Set θ = π in e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ: e^{iπ} = cos π + i sin π = −1 + 0i = −1.

So e^{iπ} + 1 = 0 — Euler's identity, linking e, i, π, 1, and 0.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Multiplying complex numbers ADDS their arguments (angles) and MULTIPLIES their moduli. In polar form, multiplication is rotation-and-scaling, not component-wise multiplication.

📊 FIGURE — e^(iθ) walks the unit circle
Euler’s formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ says: the angle θ picks a point on the unit circle whose shadow on the real axis is cos θ and on the imaginary axis is sin θ. Multiplying complex numbers adds these angles — rotation made algebraic.
"}, "COMPLEX/ch1/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A complex function w = f(z) maps the plane to the plane. Understanding these mappings and their limits sets up the central idea: differentiability, which in ℂ is far stronger than in ℝ.

Complex function
f(z) = u(x,y) + i·v(x,y) splits into real part u and imaginary part v. Limits and continuity mirror the ℝ² definitions, but demanding differentiability (next chapter) turns out to be a very strong condition.
WORKED EXAMPLE — splitting into u and v

f(z) = z² with z = x + iy: z² = (x + iy)² = x² − y² + 2xyi.

So u(x,y) = x² − y² and v(x,y) = 2xy. These two real functions must satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations for f to be differentiable.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A limit in ℂ must exist and agree as z approaches from EVERY direction in the plane (not just left/right as in ℝ). This 2D requirement is why complex differentiability is so restrictive.

📊 FIGURE — A complex number lives in the plane
z = 3 + 4i sits 3 across and 4 up; its modulus |z| = √(3² + 4²) = 5 is the arrow’s length. The conjugate z̄ = 3 − 4i is the mirror image across the real axis — and z·z̄ = |z|² = 25, always real.
📊 FIGURE — what the real exponential does not do
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Finding the period

Using e^(z+p) = e^z·e^p, the condition e^(z+p) = e^z for all z requires e^p = 1. By Euler's formula with p = 2πi:

e^(2πi) = cos 2π + i sin 2π = 1 + 0i = 1

So p = 2πi works, and the complex exponential is periodic with period 2πi. (The full set of solutions is p = 2πik for any nonzero integer k.)

Note the direction: the period is along the imaginary axis. The real exponential eˣ is strictly increasing and never repeats, so this periodicity has no real-variable analogue — and it is the reason the complex logarithm is multivalued and needs a branch cut.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The complex exponential satisfies e^(z + 2πi) = e^z, so its period is 2πi — purely imaginary. This is a genuinely new behaviour with no counterpart for eˣ on the reals, and it is what forces the complex logarithm to be multivalued.
"}, "COMPLEX/ch2/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A function that's complex-differentiable on an open region is analytic — and analyticity is astonishingly powerful: it forces the function to be infinitely differentiable and equal to its Taylor series. The test is the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

Cauchy–Riemann
f = u + iv is analytic only if u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x (with continuous partials). Consequence: u and v are HARMONIC (u_xx + u_yy = 0).
WORKED EXAMPLE — testing analyticity

f(z) = z² gives u = x² − y², v = 2xy. Check: u_x = 2x, v_y = 2x ✓; u_y = −2y, v_x = 2y, and u_y = −v_x ✓.

Both equations hold everywhere, so z² is analytic (entire). Contrast f(z) = z̄ = x − iy: u_x = 1 but v_y = −1, so CR fails — z̄ is NOT analytic.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The conjugate function f(z) = z̄ is continuous everywhere but analytic NOWHERE — Cauchy–Riemann fails. Complex differentiability is far more restrictive than real differentiability.

📊 FIGURE — Cauchy–Riemann: one complex derivative, two real equations
Write f = u + iv. Complex differentiability forces the partials to lock together: u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x. Geometrically, analytic maps preserve angles (conformal) — tiny squares go to tiny squares, just rotated and scaled.
"}, "COMPLEX/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Integrating along paths in the plane leads to two miracles: Cauchy's theorem (the integral of an analytic function around a closed loop is ZERO) and the Cauchy integral formula (a function's inside values are determined by its boundary values).

Cauchy's theorem & formula
If f is analytic inside and on a simple closed contour C, then ∮_C f(z) dz = 0. And f(a) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z−a) dz — boundary values fix interior values.
WORKED EXAMPLE — Cauchy's theorem in action

∮_C z² dz around ANY closed loop = 0, because z² is analytic everywhere (no singularities inside).

But ∮_C (1/z) dz around a loop enclosing 0 = 2πi — the singularity at 0 makes it nonzero. Singularities are where the action is.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Cauchy's theorem gives 0 only when the function is analytic EVERYWHERE inside the contour. A singularity inside the loop (like 1/z at 0) breaks it — and that's exactly what makes residues useful.

📊 FIGURE — Only enclosed singularities matter
The left contour encloses no singularity: by Cauchy’s theorem its integral is 0. The right contour wraps the pole (×): the integral picks up 2πi times the residue. Deforming a contour without crossing a pole never changes the answer.
"}, "COMPLEX/ch2/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The residue theorem is the crown jewel: it evaluates contour integrals by summing simple 'residues' at the enclosed singularities — and slays real integrals that resist every ordinary technique.

Residue theorem
∮_C f dz = 2πi · (sum of residues of f at the poles inside C). For a simple pole at z₀: Res = lim_{z→z₀} (z − z₀)f(z).
WORKED EXAMPLE — computing a residue

For f(z) = 1/(z − 3), the residue at the simple pole z = 3 is lim_{z→3}(z−3)·1/(z−3) = 1.

So ∮_C f dz = 2πi·(1) = 2πi for any contour enclosing 3, and 0 for a contour that doesn't.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Only poles INSIDE the contour contribute to the sum. A pole outside C adds nothing (Cauchy's theorem applies to it). Always check which singularities the contour actually encloses.

📊 FIGURE — Only enclosed singularities matter
The left contour encloses no singularity: by Cauchy’s theorem its integral is 0. The right contour wraps the pole (×): the integral picks up 2πi times the residue. Deforming a contour without crossing a pole never changes the answer.
"}, "COMPLEX/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Write every number as z = a + bi with i² = -1.

  • Add/subtract: combine real and imaginary parts separately.
  • Multiply: use FOIL and replace i² = -1: (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i.
  • Divide: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: (a+bi)/(c+di) = (a+bi)(c-di)/(c²+d²).
  • Modulus: |z| = √(a²+b²). Also z·z̄ = |z|² where z̄ = a-bi.
  • Argument: the angle θ with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant.

De Moivre

With z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), powers are zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ). The n distinct nth roots of r·e^(iθ) are r^(1/n)·e^(i(θ+2πk)/n) for k = 0,1,…,n-1.

Mini-example

Compute (1+i)²: here (1+i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 2i. Its modulus is √(1+1)=√2 and argument π/4, so De Moivre gives the same result: (√2)²·(cos(π/2)+i sin(π/2)) = 2i.

"}, "COMPLEX/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Euler's formula: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, so r·e^(iθ) = r cos θ + i·r sin θ converts polar to rectangular form. Key values: e^(iπ) = -1, e^(iπ/2) = i.

Residue at a simple pole

If z₀ is a simple pole of f(z) = g(z)/h(z), then Res(f, z₀) = g(z₀)/h'(z₀), or equivalently lim_{z→z₀} (z - z₀)f(z).

Residue theorem

For a closed contour enclosing poles z₁,…,z_k: ∮ f(z) dz = 2πi · Σ Res(f, z_j).

Cauchy–Riemann

For f = u + iv to be analytic: ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = -∂v/∂x.

Mini-example

Residue of 1/(z-3) at z = 3 is 1, so ∮_{|z|=5} dz/(z-3) = 2πi·1 = 2πi. And mapping z = 1+i under f(z)=z² gives (1+i)² = 2i.

"}, "COMPLEX/solving2/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Write a complex number as z = a + bi where i² = -1. Add by combining real parts and imaginary parts. Multiply using the distributive rule and replace i² with -1. To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Modulus, argument, conjugate

  • Modulus: |z| = √(a² + b²)
  • Argument: arg z = atan2(b, a)
  • Conjugate: z̄ = a - bi, and z · z̄ = a² + b² = |z|²

Polar form and De Moivre

Write z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ. Then powers follow De Moivre's theorem:

zⁿ = rⁿ (cos nθ + i sin nθ)

The nth roots of r cis θ are r^(1/n) cis((θ + 360°k)/n) for k = 0, 1, …, n-1.

Worked example

Compute (2 + 3i)(1 + 2i). Expand: 2 + 4i + 3i + 6i². Since i² = -1, this is 2 + 7i - 6 = -4 + 7i. The common mistake is forgetting the -6, which gives 8 + 7i.

"}, "COMPLEX/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Euler's formula links exponentials to trig: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. Special values include e^(iπ) = -1 and e^(iπ/2) = i. A number r e^(iθ) converts to rectangular form as r cos θ + i r sin θ.

Residues and contour integrals

At a simple pole z = z₀, the residue is

Res = lim (z → z₀) (z - z₀) f(z)

The residue theorem gives, for a contour enclosing the pole,

∮ f(z) dz = 2πi · (sum of enclosed residues)

Cauchy-Riemann

Write f = u + iv. Analyticity requires ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = -∂v/∂x. For f(z) = z², u = x² - y² and v = 2xy.

Worked example

Find the residue of z/((z-1)(z+3)) at z = 1. Multiply by (z - 1) and set z = 1: 1/(1 + 3) = 1/4. Then a contour around only this pole gives 2πi · (1/4) = πi/2.

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). \n

\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app

TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.
